clue.text: Unstraps a little sarong shifting in warm spots

indicators.note: only a small bit of the word is wanted, so just its opening letter is taken
letters that are shifting move about and change places, so the order is rearranged

blocks.note: the verb read without its final S, which appears to be a misprint since the sarong supplies that letter
the first letter of the garment

explanation.surface: Someone loosening a sarong while lounging in the sunshine.
explanation.walkthrough: The printed 'Unstraps' already carries its own S, so the clue reads best as UNSTRAP plus the S from sarong, all rearranged into SUNTRAPS.
explanation.definitionFit: A suntrap is a sheltered sunny place that catches and holds heat, hence a cosy outdoor location.

clue.text: Sneaky, frequently hiding piano

indicators.note: something hiding another keeps it tucked away inside itself

blocks.note: sly means sneaky
oft is an old word for often

explanation.surface: Someone sneakily concealing a piano, which is absurd given its size.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Piano' looks like the instrument being hidden, but it is the musical direction and the definition; oft is an old poetic form of often.
explanation.definitionFit: In music, piano is the Italian direction to play quietly, which is the adverb meaning gently and quietly.

clue.text: Tease a little weak-kneed learner

indicators.note: just a small portion of the following words is wanted, a run of letters sitting inside them

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of the first word and start of the second

explanation.surface: Mocking a nervous, timid pupil a bit.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer sits across kNEED LEarner, ignoring the hyphen and space.
explanation.definitionFit: To needle someone is to provoke or annoy them with persistent jibes, the same as teasing.

clue.text: First-year divinity student's a sweetie!

blocks.note: RE is religious education, the school subject of divinity
a fresher is a first-year university student

explanation.surface: Praising a new theology student as a lovely person.
explanation.walkthrough: A first-year divinity student is a fresher in RE. 'Sweetie' looks like a term of endearment but means a sweet; Refreshers are a British fizzy chewy sweet.
explanation.definitionFit: Refreshers are a long-standing British brand of fruity fizzy candy, so one is literally a sweet.

clue.text: Upon swell, exercising rowers – what each must do?

indicators.note: exercising puts things through their paces and works them around, so the letters are moved

blocks.note: taken as written
an eight is a rowing crew of eight oarsmen

explanation.surface: A rowing crew training on choppy water, each member needing to contribute.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rowers' gives EIGHT, the crew in a racing boat, which joins the first two words in the mix. The phrase is literally true of oarsmen in an eight.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means doing a fair share of the work, which is the duty of every team member.

clue.text: Primarily, full lists of regions' Amaryllidacaea, etc!

definitions.text: Primarily, full lists of regions' Amaryllidacaea, etc!

indicators.note: primarily means firstly, so the opening letter of each following word is taken

blocks.clueFragment: full lists of regions' Amaryllidacaea, etc
blocks.note: the initial letters of the six words

explanation.surface: A botanist describing comprehensive catalogues of a region's plants, such as the amaryllis family.
explanation.walkthrough: The heads of six words spell the answer, and the whole clue also describes it: Amaryllidaceae is the amaryllis and daffodil family of plants.
explanation.definitionFit: A flora is a complete catalogue of the plant species of a district, and these plurals are full listings.

clue.text: Help large English dog that's upset

indicators.note: in a down clue, upset means turned upside down, so the letters read from bottom to top

blocks.note: L is the abbreviation for large
E is the abbreviation for English
a pug is a small snub-nosed breed

explanation.surface: Coming to the aid of a big, distressed English hound.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the dog is overturned; the abbreviations stay in place above it.
explanation.definitionFit: A leg-up is a boost or assistance, originally a hand helping someone mount a horse.

clue.text: Primitive painter showing topless bride's outfit

indicators.note: in a down clue the top is the first letter, so without a top it loses its opening letter

blocks.note: a trousseau is the clothes and linen a bride collects for her marriage

explanation.surface: A risqué image of an artist depicting a bride in a revealing outfit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Topless' suggests something racy, but it simply removes the T from TROUSSEAU.
explanation.definitionFit: Henri Rousseau was a French self-taught artist of the naive or primitive school, famous for jungle scenes.

clue.text: One writes 19th letter a year before first

blocks.note: S is the nineteenth letter of the alphabet, spelt out
taken as written
Y is the abbreviation for year
1st, with the digit read as the letter I

explanation.surface: Someone composing letters, perhaps a schoolchild learning the alphabet in year one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Before' just puts the pieces in order. Reading the 1 of 1ST as the letter I is a common crossword trick.
explanation.definitionFit: An essayist is an author of short prose pieces, so a person who produces written work.

clue.text: Does roast with beef, batter and timing advice for chef?

indicators.note: roasting cooks and transforms ingredients, so the letters are altered into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A recipe for roast beef with batter pudding, and a tip on cooking times.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Does' looks like a verb, and 'roast' looks like the dish, but 'roast' cooks up the letters of the three words. Every ingredient word here is fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: The date stamped on packaging tells a cook how long food stays at its peak, a kind of timing guidance.

clue.text: Tense, like a guitar neck?

blocks.note: first meaning: anxious and worried
second meaning, read whimsically: full of frets, the ridges across a fingerboard

explanation.walkthrough: The second reading splits the word into its parts, as if meaning 'full of frets'; the question mark flags the play.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone fretful is uneasy and agitated, and a guitar's fingerboard carries many metal frets along it.

clue.text: They're seen with soldiers, say, getting George Cross: happy times

blocks.note: e.g. means for example, as does say
GC is the abbreviation for the George Cross medal
ups, as in ups and downs, are good times

explanation.surface: Troops being awarded a gallantry medal amid cheerful days.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Soldiers' suggests troops, but in Britain soldiers are strips of toast dipped into a soft-boiled egg. The George Cross is a British award for bravery.
explanation.definitionFit: Boiled eggs sit in small holders at breakfast, served alongside toast strips for dipping.

clue.text: Sides of langoustine consumed ... off-colour in French city

indicators.note: the sides of a word are its two edges, so only the outer letters are kept
what has consumed something has taken it inside, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: the first and last letters of the shellfish
off-colour means unwell

explanation.surface: Feeling sick after eating shellfish while in France.
explanation.walkthrough: The outer letters of langoustine wrap around ILL, as if the shellfish's edges had swallowed the illness.
explanation.definitionFit: Lille is a large city in northern France near the Belgian border.

clue.text: US cop story, not right to reboot film

indicators.note: not means without, so the following letter is removed
to reboot is to restart in a fresh configuration, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written
R is the abbreviation for right, removed from the story

explanation.surface: A studio remaking an American police drama as a new movie.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Film' is the definition, not part of the reboot story. With R gone, US COP STOY rearranges into the title.
explanation.definitionFit: Octopussy is a 1983 James Bond movie starring Roger Moore.

clue.text: Sees chest heaving, having eaten undercooked snack

indicators.note: something heaving rises and falls and churns, so its letters are thrown about
what has eaten something holds it inside, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: taken as written
raw food is not cooked enough

explanation.surface: Someone notices their chest heaving after eating underdone food.
explanation.walkthrough: The scrambled nine letters swallow RAW just before their final S.
explanation.definitionFit: Cheese straws are thin baked sticks of cheesy pastry, a savoury nibble served with drinks.

clue.text: Model superlatively lusty: most problematic

blocks.note: the Model T was Ford's famous car
horny means lusty, and the superlative form is the -est one

explanation.surface: Describing a fashion model as the most lustful and troublesome.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Model' suggests a person on a catwalk, but it gives T from the Model T Ford.
explanation.definitionFit: A thorny issue is difficult and contentious, so the superlative means most difficult.

clue.text: He painted his mum, a referee at times

blocks.note: first meaning: the American artist whose best-known portrait is of his mother
second meaning: one who blows a whistle, as a referee does

explanation.walkthrough: James McNeill Whistler's 'Arrangement in Grey and Black No. 1' is popularly called Whistler's Mother.
explanation.definitionFit: The artist's surname, and a literal description of an official who blows a whistle to stop play.

clue.text: A Queen's wavy patterns in wardrobes

blocks.note: taken as written
R is for Regina, Latin for queen
moiré is a rippled pattern on silk or other fabric

explanation.surface: A monarch's clothes cupboards hold fabrics with rippled designs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like a container signal but here only links wordplay to definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An armoire is a tall freestanding cupboard for clothes, the French-derived name for this furniture.

clue.text: How rotor-head's spinning is a problem

indicators.note: spinning whirls things round, so the letters are tumbled into another order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written, hyphen ignored

explanation.surface: A helicopter engineer worried that the rotor hub turning is a fault.
explanation.walkthrough: 'How' looks like a question word but is part of the fodder; the 's means is.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes a difficult task or tough situation, an arduous undertaking.

clue.text: Country's athletic club taking in judo practitioner, amateur ascendant

indicators.note: to take something in is to hold it inside, so one piece goes within another
in a down clue, rising means reading from bottom to top

blocks.note: AC is the abbreviation for athletic club
a dan is a grade of black belt in judo, and a holder of one
A is the abbreviation for amateur

explanation.surface: A national sports club welcoming a judoka, an unpaid athlete on the rise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ascendant' sounds like the amateur's career rising, but in a down clue it turns the whole assembly upside down, not just the last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Canada is the large North American nation north of the United States.

clue.text: A second spring besides

blocks.note: taken as written
S is the abbreviation for second
a spring is a source of water, as is a well

explanation.surface: Another spring season, in addition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spring' suggests the season, but it is a water source.
explanation.definitionFit: Both expressions mean in addition or also, adding a further item.

clue.text: In home counties these days, smallest part unsullied

indicators.note: what goes in something sits inside it, so these pieces go within another

blocks.note: the home counties surround London in the South East of England
now means at present
a whit is the least amount, as in not a whit

explanation.surface: Claiming that the outer suburbs of London are untouched by modern grime.
explanation.walkthrough: The home counties are the counties surrounding London, in the South East of England, so they give the compass abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Something as pale as fresh snow is pure and spotless, untainted by dirt.

clue.text: Loudly call for squeeze

indicators.note: something said loudly is spoken out, so we go by sound rather than spelling

blocks.note: to ring is to phone or call someone

explanation.surface: Shouting out a demand for a squeeze, perhaps a hug.
explanation.walkthrough: The silent W makes the spelling differ while the sound matches; 'call' is a telephone call.
explanation.definitionFit: To wring is to twist and compress something, such as wet laundry, to force liquid out.

clue.text: Some nonlinear systems offering approaches

indicators.note: some means a portion, so only part of the following letters is used

blocks.note: the letters straddle the end of the first word and start of the second

explanation.surface: Certain mathematical models that are not linear provide methods.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Approaches' looks like a noun meaning methods, but it is the verb, matching the -S answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To near something is to come closer to it, so this verb form equals comes closer.

clue.text: 'Podgy' (mostly fat) servicemen getting starter of hamburgers

indicators.note: mostly means all but a little, so the last letter is dropped
the starter is what comes first, so the opening letter is taken

blocks.note: lard is pig fat
GIs are American soldiers
the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: Soldiers growing chubby after eating burgers.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks around 'Podgy' set off the definition; GI is slang for an American soldier.
explanation.definitionFit: Podgy describes someone rather plump, and largish means fairly big in build.

clue.text: 'A very European' fury? That's mean

blocks.note: taken as written
V is the abbreviation for very
E is the abbreviation for European
rage is intense anger

explanation.surface: Someone quoting an extreme anger as typical of the continent, then calling it unkind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mean' suggests unkind, but it is the statistical sense.
explanation.definitionFit: In statistics the arithmetic mean is the sum divided by the count, the ordinary sense of an average.

clue.text: Go back into – or out of – employment

blocks.note: first meaning: sign up again for a job
second meaning: quit a post

explanation.walkthrough: 'Employment' serves both halves: re-signing puts you back into a job, resigning takes you out of one.
explanation.definitionFit: To re-sign is to put pen to a contract again; to resign is to give up a job voluntarily.

clue.text: Face cry that's voiced for pasta topping

indicators.note: voiced means spoken out, so the words are judged by their sound

blocks.note: to face someone is to meet them
to bawl is to cry loudly

explanation.surface: Confronting a shout heard while cooking spaghetti.
explanation.walkthrough: In non-rhotic British speech the two parts sound identical to the answer's halves.
explanation.definitionFit: Spaghetti is often served with rolled balls of minced beef on top in tomato sauce.
